cases.case_name: Vance v. Lincoln County Department of Public Welfare
cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination of an incarcerated mother's parental rights for substantial erosion of the parent-child relationship, holding that the petitioner must first carry the clear-and-convincing burden on a statutory ground and only then may the child's best interest be weighed.
cases.quote: Once the clear and convincing burden has been met, the best interest of the child is to be considered.

relevance.OUT-02: Supplies Mississippi's two-step termination sequence - statutory ground proved by clear and convincing evidence, then best interest - which controls every TPR petition in the state.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification remains the default until the department carries its clear-and-convincing burden, so the burden itself is what closes off the reunification track.
relevance.ACT-01: The opinion sets out Section 93-15-103(4)'s direction that permanent alternatives short of termination be selected where parental contact remains desirable, which is the frame for voluntary service planning.
relevance.ACT-04: The children were moved among the mother's brother, cousin and foster mother before the department took custody, showing how kinship arrangements are tested before the state acts.
relevance.DEC-06: The statutory preference for alternatives that end departmental supervision without terminating rights is the Mississippi analogue to a non-petition, services-only track.

cases.case_name: Lauderdale County Department of Human Services v. T.H.G.
cases.holding: The Court declined to create a child-welfare exception to the Rule 503 physician/psychotherapist-patient privilege in a termination proceeding based on the parents' mental illness, and remanded for a final determination on the petition.
cases.quote: we cannot obliterate the rights of the parents and thus decline to create an exception to Rule 503

relevance.INP-07: Controls whether a parent's medical and psychiatric records obtained in treatment can be used by the agency: in Mississippi they remain privileged even when a child's welfare is at stake.
relevance.ACT-06: Limits the agency's use of mental-health and medical treatment records when it seeks authority over a parent's or child's care.
relevance.ACT-03: The Court restates the presumption that a child's best interest lies in remaining with natural parents, the presumption any foster placement must overcome.
relevance.OUT-01: The natural-parent presumption recited here is what the department must displace before reunification is abandoned.
relevance.DEC-06: The opinion quotes the statutory instruction to choose guardianship or other alternatives that end departmental supervision where parental contact is desirable.

cases.case_name: S.R.B.R. v. Harrison County Department of Human Services
cases.holding: The Court affirmed a family court's termination of parental rights, holding that the petitioner must prove at least one of the grounds enumerated in Section 93-15-103(3) by clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: the petitioner must prove by clear and convincing evidence at least one of the grounds enumerated

relevance.ACT-04: The children had lived since 1998 with an aunt and uncle who the guardian ad litem recommended as adoptive parents, the standard Mississippi kinship-to-permanency path.
relevance.OUT-03: The guardian ad litem's weighing of durable legal custody against adoption shows how Mississippi courts choose between guardianship-style permanency and termination.

cases.case_name: D.J.L. v. Bolivar County Department of Human Services
cases.holding: The Court ordered a limited remand of a termination judgment because the guardian ad litem never interviewed the children or gave the court an independent evaluation, and directed that the guardian must file a written report or testify.
cases.quote: the guardian must submit a written report to the court during the hearing, or testify and thereby become available for cross-examination by the natural parent

relevance.DEC-05: Once the agency files a petition, Mississippi requires an appointed guardian ad litem whose independent investigation and report are a condition of a valid judgment.
relevance.ACT-02: A court-ordered plan that keeps children in departmental custody must be tested by a guardian who has independently interviewed the children and reported to the court.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed an award of custody to third-party custodians over the natural father, holding that the presumption favoring a natural parent is overcome by a clear showing of unfitness.
cases.quote: it has been stated many times that this presumption can be overcome by a clear showing that the parent is unfit

relevance.INP-05: Shows the route by which private caretakers, not the agency, bring a child's situation before a court and ask for authority over the child.
relevance.ACT-04: Sets the showing a non-parent caregiver must make before custody is placed with them rather than the parent.
relevance.OUT-03: States the unfitness showing required before a third-party custody or guardianship arrangement can become the child's permanent placement.

cases.case_name: May v. Harrison County Department of Human Services
cases.holding: The Court affirmed the youth court's termination of a mother's parental rights, holding the clear-and-convincing burden had been satisfied and rejecting her argument that durable legal custody should have been ordered instead.
cases.quote: The burden of proof in order to establish a case for termination of parental rights is clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.ACT-01: The mother's failure to complete services offered before the petition is what drove the youth court's decision, showing what a voluntary services record must contain.
relevance.ACT-02: Demonstrates how compliance with a court-supervised plan is measured against the statutory termination grounds at the next hearing.
relevance.OUT-01: The opinion canvasses the Adoption and Safe Families Act's limits on required reunification efforts in aggravated-circumstances cases.
relevance.OUT-03: Discusses durable legal custody as a non-permanent alternative to termination in which the parent retains residual rights subject to further review.

cases.holding: The Court reversed a youth court order that had terminated a mother's rights on the agency's Rule 60(b) motion, holding the evidence relied upon was not newly discovered and did not merit termination, and remanded on visitation.
cases.quote: We review the termination of parental rights to a minor child applying a “clear and convincing evidence” standard, thus applying a “clearly erroneous/manifest error” standard of review.

relevance.OUT-05: Where the agency's proof does not meet the statutory grounds, the correct outcome is that the petition fails and the earlier refusal to terminate stands.
relevance.FAIL-01: A textbook reversal: the appellate court vacated a termination that the agency had obtained by reopening a judgment on evidence that was never new.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed a chancery court judgment terminating a father's parental rights in an adoption proceeding, applying the two-prong test of a proven statutory ground followed by the child's best interest.
cases.quote: Once the first prong has been satisfied, the court must consider the second prong: the best interest of the child.

relevance.OUT-02: States the two-prong structure Mississippi chancellors apply when termination is sought inside a private adoption case.
relevance.DEC-03: The finding that grounds were proved by clear and convincing evidence is the adjudicative counterpart of an agency's substantiated finding.

cases.holding: The Court reversed a youth court's abuse adjudication and custody order because the father was never served or notified of the hearings and the court did not comply with the Youth Court Act's notice and advice-of-rights requirements.
cases.quote: The Hinds County Youth Court failed to comply with the statutory requirements to assure notice to the father for the various hearings affecting the custody of his minor son

relevance.INP-04: Illustrates how an emergency order and court-driven hearings open a youth court file and what the court must do at the first appearance.
relevance.INP-10: When a screening becomes a formal youth court proceeding, the statutory notice and advice-of-rights steps attach immediately.
relevance.DEC-02: Acceptance of a case for formal action triggers service of process on every required party, including a non-custodial father.
relevance.DEC-05: A petition that proceeds without service on a required parent cannot support an adjudication.
relevance.ACT-05: The youth court's protective response was to place the child with the non-offending mother after finding abuse by the father, the Mississippi alternative to removal.

cases.case_name: J.C.N.F. v. Stone County Department of Human Services
cases.holding: The Court affirmed a chancellor's termination of parental rights under Section 93-15-103(3)(h), holding the findings were supported by substantial credible evidence and free of manifest error.
cases.quote: this Court will affirm a chancellor's findings of fact if there is substantial credible evidence to support them, unless there is manifest error

relevance.OUT-02: States the deferential standard a parent must overcome on appeal from a termination judgment in Mississippi.
relevance.DEC-03: Shows how the trial-level finding of a statutory ground, once supported by credible evidence, becomes practically unreviewable.

cases.case_name: A.B. v. Lauderdale County Department of Human Services
cases.holding: The Court reversed a termination of parental rights, holding the department's circumstantial proof of parental drug use and neglect did not amount to clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: The party seeking termination of parental rights must prove grounds for termination by “clear and convincing evidence.”

relevance.DEC-01: Circumstantial suspicion of drug use, including a refused hair test, is not a substitute for proof and cannot sustain agency conclusions.
relevance.DEC-03: Directly limits what an agency may treat as substantiated: inference about drug use, without documentary proof, falls short.
relevance.OUT-05: Where proof fails, the case must end in the parent's favor rather than in permanency planning away from the family.
relevance.FAIL-01: A reversal of an agency-obtained termination for insufficiency of the agency's own evidence.

cases.holding: The Court held the chancery court properly had subject-matter jurisdiction over a guardianship petition after the youth court voluntarily terminated its own jurisdiction under Section 43-21-151(2).
cases.quote: The plain language of the Act does allow the youth court to terminate its jurisdiction of a case.

relevance.INP-04: Shows a youth court moving a child's custody question to another court, the mechanism by which judicial referral reshapes who decides.
relevance.INP-05: Private petitioners, not the agency, opened this matter and later sought to undo it, the classic guardian-request entry point.
relevance.INP-11: The exclusive-and-priority-jurisdiction analysis is the state-law template for deciding which forum controls when jurisdictional claims compete.
relevance.ACT-04: Kin who seek custody of a child already before the youth court must litigate in whichever forum retains jurisdiction.
relevance.OUT-03: Guardianship as a permanency outcome in Mississippi runs through chancery court, which can only act once youth court jurisdiction ends.
relevance.OUT-04: Section 43-21-151(2), the provision fixing the outer bound of youth court jurisdiction over a child, is construed here.

cases.case_name: Cruz v. Jackson County Department of Human Services
cases.holding: The Court affirmed the youth court's order keeping its records confidential but reversed and rendered as to a gag order barring participants from discussing the case, finding no compelling state interest supported it.
cases.quote: We find that the youth court did not abuse its discretion in ordering that its records remain confidential.

relevance.INP-09: A mother separated from her newborn for over a year could speak publicly about the case, which is how systemic problems reach oversight bodies.
relevance.FAIL-06: Distinguishes lawful record confidentiality from an unlawful prior restraint on the parties themselves.
relevance.PMC-03: Participants' ability to speak about their own youth court case is the practical precondition to citizen review of agency conduct.
relevance.PMC-05: Records stay confidential, but a court may not silence the people who lived the case; that line governs transparency demands in Mississippi.
relevance.PMC-06: Public analysis of child-welfare outcomes depends on the parties' First Amendment right recognized here, since the files themselves stay closed.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed the award of custody to the natural father over the maternal grandmother and declined to change the established grounds for rebutting the natural-parent presumption.
cases.quote: we find no legally compelling reason to alter or abandon our established standards for rebuttal of the natural-parent presumption

relevance.INP-05: A relative caregiver's petition is measured against the parent's presumptive right, which shapes what a guardian's request for help can achieve.
relevance.ACT-04: Kinship placement cannot displace a fit parent absent abandonment, desertion, immoral conduct or unfitness proved by clear and convincing evidence.
relevance.OUT-03: Sets the boundary between kinship permanency and the constitutionally protected position of the natural parent.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of J.T. v. Hinds County Youth Court
cases.holding: The Court reversed a youth court's adjudication that a three-year-old had been sexually abused as unsupported by sufficient evidence, and confirmed that the Mississippi Rules of Evidence govern youth court adjudicatory hearings.
cases.quote: except where specifically superseded by a youth-court-specific rule, the Mississippi Rules of Evidence apply with full force and effect

relevance.INP-01: A child's single statement, reported onward by professionals, is where the chain began, and the Court measured what that report could prove.
relevance.INP-02: Shows the evidentiary weight a third-party account of a child's disclosure carries once the case reaches adjudication.
relevance.INP-03: The forensic interview at the children's advocacy center and the law-enforcement-linked investigation are assessed for reliability, not accepted on their face.
relevance.INP-07: The children's justice center medical examination report was admitted over hearsay objection, and the Court holds such reports must satisfy the Rules of Evidence.
relevance.DEC-03: A substantiated finding of abuse cannot rest on hearsay that fits no exception and that the trial judge cannot verify as reliable.
relevance.ACT-05: The abuse finding against the father that would have supported protective relief was set aside for insufficient evidence.
relevance.OUT-05: Insufficient evidence at adjudication requires reversal, not a lesser disposition.
relevance.FAIL-01: The Supreme Court reversed the youth court's adjudication outright, the strongest form of judicial correction available in a Mississippi abuse case.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed a chancery judgment terminating a father's parental rights and granting the adoption petition, holding the chancellor's decision was supported by substantial credible evidence and was not manifestly wrong.
cases.quote: we find that the chancellor’s decision to terminate John’s parental rights was supported by substantial credible evidence and was not manifestly wrong

relevance.OUT-02: Shows the combined termination-and-adoption judgment that produces permanency in Mississippi chancery practice, and the deference it receives on review.

cases.case_name: E.K. v. Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services
cases.holding: The Court vacated a youth court's neglect adjudication and rendered judgment for the child, holding the parents' notice and right-to-counsel protections were violated, the petition gave no notice of the circumstances alleged, and a parent's marijuana use without a causal connection to harm is legally insufficient proof of neglect.
cases.quote: Elizabeth’s marijuana usage does not negate the requirement of a causal connection between the drug usage and the neglect.

relevance.INP-01: A report that produces nothing but a positive parental drug screen cannot carry an agency case forward on its own.
relevance.INP-10: Escalation from screening to formal adjudication must be matched by proof of actual harm, not by the fact of a positive test.
relevance.INP-12: Cites Section 43-21-301(3), which bars a probable-cause finding for a custody order based solely on a parent's positive marijuana test.
relevance.DEC-01: Defines the floor below which a report must be closed rather than pursued: drug use with no shown effect on the child.
relevance.DEC-02: Acceptance for investigation must be followed by service and an on-the-record determination of waiver and counsel rights.
relevance.DEC-03: The central Mississippi authority on what a substantiated neglect finding requires - a causal link between parental conduct and harm to the child.
relevance.DEC-04: Because a positive marijuana test alone cannot supply probable cause, it cannot support the emergency custody order that precedes removal.
relevance.DEC-05: A neglect petition that merely recites the statutory definition fails to give the parents notice of what will be adjudicated.
relevance.DEC-06: Where the evidence shows a home that 'checked out fine,' the case belongs outside the court system entirely.
relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered services imposed on the strength of a drug screen alone rest on an adjudication that cannot stand.
relevance.OUT-05: The Court rendered judgment for the child rather than remanding, the cleanest form of dismissal after a failed adjudication.
relevance.FAIL-01: Vacatur plus rendition shows the full remedial range when a youth court proceeds without notice, counsel or sufficient evidence.

cases.holding: The Court read Section 43-21-261(1) broadly and held that a criminal defendant was entitled to limited, court-supervised access to youth court records and the transcript concerning his accuser.
cases.quote: the best interest of the child, as well the proper and just functioning of our youth court system, demands that Michael have limited access to the materials he seeks

relevance.FAIL-06: Confidentiality is not absolute; a court may order limited disclosure where the statute's own exceptions are engaged.
relevance.PMC-05: The leading Mississippi statement that Section 43-21-261 contemplates disclosure in defined circumstances rather than blanket secrecy.

cases.case_name: Pass Christian School District v. Harrison County Youth Court of Mississippi
cases.holding: The Court held that youth court records and transcripts could not be released directly to a civil defendant, but reversed in part and remanded so the record could be reviewed in camera to determine what, if anything, should be disclosed.
cases.quote: Disclosure of youth-court records is subject to the discretion of the youth-court judge.

relevance.FAIL-06: Sets the procedure - in camera review rather than outright refusal - when an agency or court withholds youth court material from a litigant.
relevance.PMC-05: The most recent Mississippi Supreme Court statement on who may obtain youth court records and by what process.
relevance.PMC-06: Any external analysis of Mississippi child-welfare case files must run through the discretionary, judge-controlled disclosure regime described here.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Department of Human Services v. D.C.
cases.holding: The Court held that Section 43-15-125 immunizes the Department and its officers from claims arising out of its licensing and licensing-related investigation of a foster home, but affirmed the denial of summary judgment on the foster child's remaining Tort Claims Act allegations about his care.
cases.quote: Section 43-15-125 grants immunity to DHS for its licensing of foster homes.

relevance.INP-09: Shows how far civil litigation can reach into agency practice, and where statutory immunity blocks scrutiny of licensing decisions.
relevance.ACT-03: Licensing of the foster home in which a child is placed is immunized conduct, which shapes what a placement claim can allege.
relevance.OUT-04: Defines the Department's residual, non-immune duties toward a child who remains in its care.
relevance.OUT-06: The governing Mississippi authority on agency liability when a child is seriously harmed while in foster care.
relevance.FAIL-04: Harm to a child under agency supervision can be litigated, but not through the licensing decision that placed him there.
relevance.PMC-01: The immunity line drawn here limits what performance failures can be tested in court rather than through federal review.
relevance.PMC-02: Financial and licensing administration is insulated from damages claims, leaving audit and oversight as the remaining accountability route.
relevance.PMC-04: A serious-harm case against the Department survives in part, which is how facts about care failures become public record.

cases.holding: Reviewing the statute de novo, the Court reversed a youth court's bypass of reunification, holding that Section 43-21-603(7)(c) requires both one of the three enumerated criteria and a best-interest finding, and that a father's pre-birth criminal history was not conduct to which he subjected the child.
cases.quote: after determining that one of the first three criteria have been met, the youth court must also determine that bypassing reunification is in the best interests of the child

relevance.ACT-01: A parent cannot be written out of services on the basis of history the child was never exposed to.
relevance.ACT-02: The controlling Mississippi construction of when a youth court may order a disposition that dispenses with reasonable reunification efforts.
relevance.ACT-03: Foster placement without a reunification plan requires findings the youth court here could not make.
relevance.DEC-05: At the disposition stage that follows the petition, the statutory criteria for bypassing reunification are read strictly against the agency.
relevance.OUT-01: The most recent Mississippi authority protecting the reunification track from being bypassed on loose 'aggravated circumstances' reasoning.
relevance.FAIL-01: The Supreme Court reversed both the youth court and the Court of Appeals, correcting the standard of review as well as the statute's meaning.
relevance.FAIL-03: Section 43-21-603(7)(c) implements the federal reasonable-efforts condition on Title IV-E funding, so its misapplication is a compliance question as well as an error.

cases.holding: The Court reversed the dismissal of a failure-to-report claim against a school principal, holding that while she has qualified immunity for discretionary judgments, once reasonable cause is determined the Section 43-21-353 report is mandatory and non-discretionary.
cases.quote: if, after investigation, it was determined there was reasonable cause to support a complaint of suspected child abuse, a mandatory, non-discretionary report to the proper agency is called for

relevance.INP-01: The leading Mississippi case on the mandatory reporter's duty under Section 43-21-353 and the immunity available to the reporter who exercises judgment.
relevance.INP-02: Explains that the reporting statute reaches 'any other person having reasonable cause to suspect' abuse or neglect, not only listed professionals.
relevance.INP-06: Once reasonable cause exists, the oral report to the agency must be made immediately; the duty is not discretionary.
relevance.INP-08: Decided against a school principal, this is the controlling authority on educator reporting duties and exposure in Mississippi.
relevance.DEC-01: The reporter's threshold judgment about 'reasonable cause' is discretionary and protected, which is why screening decisions rarely generate liability.
relevance.OUT-06: A failure-to-report claim is the principal private remedy in Mississippi when a child is harmed after professionals stayed silent.
relevance.FAIL-04: Establishes that non-reporting by an official can be actionable negligence notwithstanding qualified immunity for policy-level judgments.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality and serious-injury review turns on whether mandated reports were made, a duty this case makes legally enforceable.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before terminating parental rights.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.OUT-02: The federal constitutional floor beneath Mississippi's clear-and-convincing termination standard, cited by the Mississippi Supreme Court in every leading TPR case.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County, North Carolina
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Constitution does not require appointed counsel in every parental termination proceeding and left the decision to the trial court in the first instance, subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: leave the decision whether due process calls for the appointment of counsel for indigent parents in termination proceedings to be answered in the first instance by the trial court

relevance.OUT-02: Sets the federal baseline on counsel in termination cases; Mississippi goes further by statute, giving parties a right to counsel at all stages of a youth court proceeding.
relevance.DEC-05: When a petition is filed, the federal floor is a case-by-case counsel inquiry, which Mississippi's Youth Court Act supplements with an express advice-of-rights duty.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Reversing the Mississippi Supreme Court, the Court held that Mississippi could not condition an indigent parent's appeal from a decree terminating her parental rights on her ability to prepay record-preparation fees.
cases.quote: we hold that Mississippi may not withhold from M. L. B. “a ‘record of sufficient completeness’ to permit proper [appellate] consideration of [her] claims.”

relevance.FAIL-01: A Mississippi case: appellate correction of a termination decree cannot be priced out of reach of an indigent parent.
relevance.PMC-05: Access to the record of one's own termination case is a constitutional entitlement, not an agency courtesy.
relevance.PMC-06: Any accountability analysis of Mississippi terminations depends on appellate records being obtainable by the parents who lived them.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative constitutional duty on a State to protect a child from private violence, even where the agency knew of the danger and failed to act.
cases.quote: we conclude that a State’s failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause

relevance.FAIL-03: Failures to meet federal performance expectations are not, by themselves, constitutional violations remediable by the affected family.
relevance.FAIL-04: The controlling barrier to constitutional damages claims when a child is killed or maimed after the agency failed to act on known danger.
relevance.OUT-06: Defines what a family can and cannot recover under federal law after a child dies in circumstances the agency was monitoring.
relevance.PMC-01: Because the Constitution supplies no remedy for failure to protect, federal monitoring and state-law remedies carry the accountability load.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality review exists precisely because the judicial remedy foreclosed here leaves no other public accounting.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that ICWA domicile is defined by federal law, that twins born off the reservation took the reservation domicile of their parents, and that the Choctaw tribal court therefore had exclusive jurisdiction, vacating the Mississippi adoption decree.
cases.quote: In enacting the ICWA Congress confirmed that, in child custody proceedings involving Indian children domiciled on the reservation, tribal jurisdiction was exclusive as to the States.

relevance.INP-11: The controlling authority for Mississippi: a Choctaw child domiciled on the reservation cannot be adopted through state court, however the parents arrange the birth.
relevance.FAIL-05: State courts may not use parental choice of forum to defeat the tribal and cultural interests Congress protected in ICWA.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that ICWA Section 1912(d)'s remedial-efforts requirement applies only where termination would precipitate the breakup of an Indian family, and that Section 1912(f) and the Section 1915(a) placement preferences did not bar this adoption by a non-Indian couple.
cases.quote: Consistent with the statutory text, we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family’s “breakup” would be precipitated by the termination of the parent’s rights.

relevance.INP-11: Marks the outer limit of ICWA's active-efforts and placement protections when the Indian parent never had custody of the child.
relevance.ACT-04: Holds Section 1915(a)'s placement preferences inapplicable where no alternative Indian family has formally sought to adopt, which constrains tribal kinship-placement claims.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that removing a child from a parent's custody because of the racial composition of the parent's household violates the Equal Protection Clause.
cases.quote: Private biases may be outside the reach of the law, but the law cannot, directly or indirectly, give them effect.

relevance.FAIL-05: The governing federal rule when a placement or custody decision is driven by race or by anticipated community prejudice.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the 'reasonable efforts' requirement of the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act creates no federally enforceable right and cannot be enforced by private plaintiffs under Section 1983 or an implied right of action.
cases.quote: § 671(a)(15) does not create a federally enforceable right to “reasonable efforts” under §1983

relevance.INP-09: Because private enforcement is unavailable, federal review and the Secretary's plan-approval process are the operative oversight mechanisms.
relevance.FAIL-03: The decisive federal authority: a state's failure to make reasonable efforts is remediable administratively, not by suit from the affected families.
relevance.PMC-01: Explains why CFSR findings and program improvement plans, not litigation, are the lever on state performance.
relevance.PMC-02: Financial conditions attached to Title IV-E are enforced through the Secretary and audit, which is where accountability data originates.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review panels matter precisely because the statute they review confers no privately enforceable right.
relevance.PMC-06: Any outside analysis of state compliance must be framed as advocacy to federal overseers rather than as a litigable claim.

cases.case_name: Gates v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
cases.holding: Affirming summary judgment on qualified-immunity grounds, the court held prospectively that the Fourth Amendment governs child-abuse investigations, that the government may not seize a child absent a court order, parental consent or exigent circumstances, and that an uncorroborated anonymous tip will rarely justify seizing a child.
cases.quote: an anonymous tip regarding child abuse will rarely be sufficient to justify the seizure of a child

relevance.INP-02: A third-party report standing alone does not authorize state action against the child; corroboration is what converts a tip into grounds.
relevance.INP-03: Sets the Fifth Circuit rule for investigations conducted jointly by caseworkers and deputies, including entries and child interviews.
relevance.INP-06: The controlling circuit authority on how much weight an anonymous hotline tip can bear before a child is seized.
relevance.INP-08: Children removed for interview at school are seized within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment, which governs school-based investigative contacts.
relevance.INP-12: Protective custody without a court order requires consent or exigency, defined as reasonable cause to believe the child faces imminent physical or sexual abuse at home.
relevance.DEC-02: Governs how an accepted report may be investigated in Mississippi's federal circuit: warrantless entry requires consent or exigency.
relevance.DEC-04: The leading Fifth Circuit statement of the constitutional standard for an emergency removal decision.
relevance.ACT-05: A court order is the ordinary lawful instrument for protective intervention; its absence must be justified by consent or exigency.
relevance.FAIL-02: The case Mississippi Section 1983 plaintiffs must satisfy: no court order, no consent and no exigency means an unconstitutional seizure.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of qualified immunity to the caseworker who removed two boys not named in the court order and with no evidence of imminent danger, holding that requirement was clearly established before Gates, while reversing as to the search and the supervisor.
cases.quote: Gates was not required to give social workers fair notice that imminent danger must exist before a child may be removed without a warrant or court order

relevance.INP-12: Confirms that emergency custody of a child not covered by a court order demands independent evidence of imminent danger.
relevance.DEC-04: A cluttered home and accessible medications, without more, do not make a removal decision constitutionally defensible.
relevance.ACT-05: A court order authorizing action as to one child does not authorize seizure of that child's siblings.
relevance.ACT-06: Arose from the parents' refusal to consent to radiation treatment, the classic medical-neglect trigger for emergency intervention.
relevance.FAIL-02: Denial of qualified immunity here is the clearest Fifth Circuit example of a removal that crossed the constitutional line.

cases.case_name: Roe v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held the caseworker's entry was covered by the mother's earlier consent to a home visit and reversed the denial of qualified immunity, while holding that affirmative verbal consent is required for an investigative home entry and that silence or passivity is not consent.
cases.quote: Although they still must obtain the parent’s verbal, affirmative consent before conducting an investigative home interview, they need not obtain that consent again when they appear at the parent’s doorstep.

relevance.INP-03: Defines what a caseworker arriving with or after a law-enforcement referral may do at the door without a warrant.
relevance.INP-06: The investigation began with a report to the agency, and the court examines how far that report alone lets the state into the home.
relevance.INP-07: Holds that a visual body-cavity search or examination of a child in non-exigent circumstances requires a warrant or valid consent.
relevance.DEC-02: The operative Fifth Circuit rule on consent for the investigative home visit that follows acceptance of a report.
relevance.ACT-06: Where circumstances are not exigent, the worker has time to obtain a warrant or have a physician conduct any intimate examination.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that a teacher who fabricated evidence of sexual abuse, causing a three-year removal and state-initiated termination proceedings, violated the clearly established right to family integrity and was not entitled to qualified immunity.
cases.quote: We therefore hold that Plaintiffs' claims fall squarely within the well established constitutional right to family integrity and to be free of arbitrary, oppressive governmental action.

relevance.INP-08: The report that started the case came from a teacher and was fabricated; this is the outer bound of educator reporting protection.
relevance.DEC-03: A substantiated finding built on manufactured evidence is not protected by immunity at any level of the system.
relevance.FAIL-02: Supplies the substantive-due-process theory, distinct from the Fourth Amendment, for a prolonged wrongful separation.
relevance.FAIL-05: Arbitrary and oppressive state action against a family is actionable even when taken by a non-agency official.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
cases.holding: The court remanded the procedural-due-process claim against the caseworker while rejecting the claims against the officers, holding it is clearly established that a court order or exigency is the predeprivation process due before a child is removed.
cases.quote: It is thus clearly established that a court order or exigency is the predeprivation process that is due when social workers remove a child.

relevance.INP-12: States the process due before protective custody attaches, in the circuit that governs Mississippi.
relevance.DEC-04: The removal decision itself must be preceded by a court order unless genuine exigency excuses it.
relevance.FAIL-02: Current Fifth Circuit framing of the wrongful-removal claim as procedural due process rather than only Fourth Amendment.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed in part the denial of qualified immunity, holding that an unsuitable living situation, without evidence of imminent danger, is not exigency justifying a warrantless removal.
cases.quote: Unsuitable as R.B.’s living situation may have been, it did not constitute exigent circumstances necessitating warrantless removal from his mother.

relevance.INP-12: The most recent circuit authority separating poor conditions from the imminent danger that authorizes protective custody.
relevance.DEC-04: Drug use and violence in a home are concerning but do not by themselves establish exigency for removal.
relevance.ACT-03: Foster placement entered without exigency or a court order is constitutionally infirm from the outset.
relevance.FAIL-02: Confirms in 2024 that the Gates standard remains clearly established law for wrongful-removal suits in Mississippi's circuit.

cases.holding: The Court reversed and set aside a decree allowing a stepfather to adopt over the natural father's objection, holding that abandonment, desertion or unfitness must be proved by clear and convincing evidence before the child's best interest may be considered, and that the Holifields had not carried that burden.
cases.quote: Once that has been established, the best interest of the child is to be considered.

relevance.OUT-02: The origin of Mississippi's two-prong rule for severing parental rights - a statutory ground proved by clear and convincing evidence, and only then the child's best interest - which Vance, W.A.S. and S.R.B.R. each restate by citing this case.
relevance.DEC-03: Fixes the order of proof behind any founded conclusion that a parent should lose the child: the ground must be established first, and the welfare judgment may not be used to supply what the proof lacks.

cases.case_name: G.Q.A. v. Harrison County Department of Human Services
cases.holding: The Court affirmed a family court judgment terminating both parents' rights to a severely burned and malnourished child, holding that family court terminations are reviewed under the same clear-and-convincing standard as chancery terminations and that the findings of serial abuse and substantial erosion of the relationship were supported by substantial evidence.
cases.quote: A Family Court judgment concerning termination of parental rights will be reviewed under the same standard as a Chancery Court judgment, which is clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.OUT-02: The leading Mississippi statement of the termination standard of review, uniform across chancery and family courts, and the authority later cases cite for it.
relevance.OUT-01: Sets out the Adoption and Safe Families Act provision that reasonable efforts to reunite are not required once a court finds the parent subjected the child to aggravated circumstances - the federal limit on the reunification track that May later applies.
relevance.ACT-04: Rejects the parents' request that custody instead go to the paternal grandparents who were raising the siblings, showing that the sibling-unity and kinship preferences yield where the child's medical and developmental needs point elsewhere.
relevance.DEC-03: Shows what a founded finding of serial abuse rests on in Mississippi - expert medical testimony, physical evidence and exhibits across numerous hearings - rather than inference.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed the youth court's grant of durable legal custody of a chronically abused child to her long-time foster parents, but reversed the portion of the judgment permanently relieving the Department of Human Services of any further involvement, holding that durable legal custody leaves the parents' residual rights intact and ends only the mandatory annual dispositional reviews, not the youth court's jurisdiction or the Department's ability to monitor.
cases.quote: The fact that under durable legal custody the parent retains some form of residual rights and responsibilities is a vital and obvious distinction to termination of parental rights.

relevance.OUT-03: The Supreme Court's construction of durable legal custody under Sections 43-21-609 and 43-21-613, Mississippi's guardianship-style permanency device, which the youth court itself described as similar to a chancery guardianship.
relevance.OUT-04: Holds that a durable legal custody disposition does not oust the youth court of continuing jurisdiction over the child or foreclose further dispositional review hearings as needed.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification may be set aside in favour of durable legal custody where the youth court determines on the evidence before it that returning the child is not in her best interest.
relevance.ACT-02: Shows how a court-supervised permanency plan is converted into a disposition, and the four options - return to parent, relative placement, termination, durable legal custody - the agency and court must weigh.
relevance.ACT-03: A long-term foster placement became the child's permanency outcome without terminating the mother's residual rights or her supervised visitation.

cases.holding: The Court reversed and remanded a circuit court order transferring an indicted juvenile to youth court, holding among other things that the judge abused his discretion by obtaining the youth court and school records for in camera inspection while denying both parties any access to them.
cases.quote: The judge does have discretion to determine the extent and purpose of disclosure. However, he abused his discretion in this case by keeping all records from the parties

relevance.FAIL-06: Withholding youth court records entirely from the parties, instead of fixing the extent and purpose of disclosure, is an abuse of discretion and defeats appellate review of the decision that relied on them.
relevance.PMC-05: The authority on which Pass Christian rests: Section 43-21-261 places disclosure of youth court records in the judge's calibrated discretion rather than placing them beyond reach.
relevance.PMC-06: Any outside review of Mississippi youth court material must be obtained through a judge's disclosure order, since the records are neither open nor absolutely closed.

cases.holding: The Court reversed an educational-neglect adjudication, the ensuing neglect adjudication and a contempt citation and returned the child to her parents, holding that the Youth Court Act imposes a mandatory duty on the judge to advise the parties of their right to counsel and to explain the purpose of each adjudicatory hearing, and that noncompliance is reversible error.
cases.quote: The youth court did not inform I.G.'s mother and step-father of their right to counsel, as mandated by our legislature, and for this reason the cause must be reversed.

relevance.INP-04: Shows a compulsory-attendance referral converting into a youth court neglect case, and what the court owes the parents at that first appearance.
relevance.INP-10: Escalation from an educational-neglect petition into a general neglect adjudication must be announced to the parents under Section 43-21-557(1)(d); silent escalation is reversible error.
relevance.DEC-02: Once the petition brought the family before the youth court, the judge was bound to ascertain whether each party had counsel and to inform them of the right before taking any evidence.
relevance.DEC-05: The authority In the Interest of N.W. rests on, and the cleaner citation for the rule that a petition cannot support an adjudication where the statutory notice and advice-of-rights steps were skipped.
relevance.ACT-02: Disposition must follow a separate, distinct adjudicatory hearing, so service and placement orders entered after a blurred proceeding cannot stand.
relevance.FAIL-01: Establishes that noncompliance with the Youth Court Act's notice requirements is itself reversible error, independent of the sufficiency of the evidence.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Dissolution of the Marriage of Leverock and Hamby: Pendleton v. Leverock
cases.holding: The Court affirmed the chancellor's refusal to terminate the father's parental rights but reversed the award of custody to him, holding the record established desertion so that the natural-parent presumption was rebutted and custody had to be redetermined through an on-the-record Albright best-interests analysis.
cases.quote: This presumption in favor of a natural parent has long been recognized, and Tony is entitled to it unless there is proof that he has relinquished it.

relevance.ACT-04: The leading modern Mississippi statement of what a third-party or in loco parentis caregiver must show - abandonment, desertion or other unfitness by clear and convincing evidence - before a child can be placed with them over a natural parent.
relevance.OUT-03: Third-party permanency becomes available only once the natural-parent presumption is rebutted, and even then custody turns on an on-the-record best-interests analysis rather than on the caregiver's status.
relevance.OUT-01: Return to the natural parent does not follow automatically from a refusal to terminate; a parent who deserted the child loses the presumptive claim to custody.
relevance.INP-05: The third-party caregivers who had raised the child since infancy petitioned in their own right, the private route by which a caregiver's request for authority over a child reaches a court.

cases.holding: On interlocutory appeal the Court reversed and rendered, dismissing a chancery court termination petition for want of jurisdiction, holding that in counties with a county court sitting as youth court a prior youth court proceeding concerning the same child gives the youth court priority of jurisdiction over the chancery court.
cases.quote: Now, however, the Legislature has given both chancery and county courts acting as youth courts the power to determine whether parental rights should be terminated.

relevance.INP-11: The forum-priority rule for Mississippi child-welfare matters: where two courts could act on the same child, prior youth court involvement determines which one decides.
relevance.INP-04: A youth court that has already entered custody and visitation orders keeps the case; a later petition elsewhere cannot reopen the same child's situation in a second forum.
relevance.DEC-05: A termination petition filed in chancery court after adverse youth court rulings is dismissed outright, which is the mechanism preventing forum shopping at the petition stage.
relevance.OUT-04: Marks the boundary between the youth court's statutory jurisdiction over a child and the chancery court's constitutional jurisdiction, the analysis Guardianship of B.A.D. is written against.

cases.case_name: De La Oliva v. Lowndes County Department of Public Welfare
cases.holding: The Court reversed and rendered a judgment terminating a mother's parental rights and directed that custody of the child be restored to her, holding that the preponderance standard then prescribed by Section 93-15-109 was unconstitutional under Santosky v. Kramer and that the proof was in any event insufficient to establish abandonment or deep-seated antipathy by clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: The chancellor, in making her findings in the case sub judice, clearly relied on an unconstitutional and impermissible standard of proof.

relevance.FAIL-01: The paradigm Mississippi reversal, cited in Vance and in Petit: a termination decreed on the wrong standard of proof is manifestly wrong and is set aside outright.
relevance.OUT-05: Where the department's proof fails, the correct disposition is rendition for the parent and immediate restoration of custody, not a remand giving the agency another attempt.
relevance.ACT-02: The welfare department had been ordered by an earlier chancery decree to file a plan for the child's return, never implemented one, and moved to terminate only after the mother sued for custody - the record of a service plan that existed on paper only.

cases.case_name: Olivia Y. ex rel. Johnson v. Barbour
cases.court: United States District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi
cases.holding: In the class action challenging Mississippi's child welfare system the court granted in part and denied in part the State officials' motion to dismiss, dismissing the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act claims as conferring no privately enforceable rights, dismissing the equal-protection claims and the protective-services class's due-process claims, but allowing the in-custody children's substantive-due-process claim to constitutionally adequate care to proceed.
cases.quote: For the reasons given, the court concludes that defendants' motion to dismiss plaintiffs' claims under the AACWA should be granted.

relevance.FAIL-03: Holds that the AACWA's case-plan, case-review, placement and licensing provisions confer no rights enforceable under Section 1983, so Mississippi's federal compliance failures are not litigable by the children they affect.
relevance.PMC-01: Because AACWA compliance cannot be enforced by the children, systemic performance is addressed through the Secretary's plan-approval and review machinery and, as here, through constitutional injunctive litigation rather than statutory claims.
relevance.PMC-02: Claims built on the funding and licensing conditions attached to federal child-welfare money were dismissed, leaving financial oversight to audit and the federal agency rather than to the affected class.
relevance.OUT-06: Children harmed while in the Division of Family and Children's Services' custody retain a substantive-due-process claim to constitutionally adequate care arising from the State's special relationship with them.
relevance.FAIL-04: Separates the failed state-created-danger theory, unavailable in the Fifth Circuit for children not in custody, from the viable in-custody claim that is the route for litigating serious harm suffered in care.
relevance.INP-09: The systemic challenge to Mississippi's child welfare system, brought for children in and at risk of entering state custody, is the vehicle through which agency-wide caseload, placement and investigation practice is examined in court.

notes: All 36 cases were retrieved from CourtListener on 2026-09-20 and their opinion text read for the passage quoted; every quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the majority (or unanimous) opinion text, with only whitespace and curly-quote normalization, and each quote was checked to fall before any concurrence or dissent in the combined text.

Mississippi's abuse/neglect system runs through the Youth Court Act, Miss. Code Ann. Sections 43-21-101 et seq. (mandatory reporting at 43-21-353; custody orders and probable cause at 43-21-301; required parties, process and right to counsel at 43-21-501, -507 and -557; disposition and reasonable-efforts bypass at 43-21-603; record confidentiality at 43-21-261). Termination of parental rights is governed by Title 93, Chapter 15 (recodified 2016; older cases cite Section 93-15-103, the current statute is Sections 93-15-101 to -133).

No published Mississippi appellate decision was found on extended foster care or jurisdiction past age 18, so OUT-04 is carried by Guardianship of B.A.D. v. Finnegan (construing Section 43-21-151(2), which fixes and terminates youth court jurisdiction over a child) and MDHS v. D.C. (residual agency duties to a child in care). Treat Section 43-21-151(2) and the state's Chafee/extended-foster-care policy as the primary authority there.

No published Mississippi decision was found adopting or construing a differential/alternative response track (DEC-06); the node is served by E.K. (what evidence cannot support formal intervention) and by the statutory preference, quoted in Vance and T.H.G., for permanent alternatives that end departmental supervision without termination.

Mississippi has no state ICWA statute and no reported Mississippi Supreme Court decision applying ICWA's active-efforts, qualified-expert-witness or transfer provisions since Holyfield. INP-11 therefore rests on the federal standard: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield (itself a Mississippi case) and Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl, plus the state-law forum analysis in Guardianship of B.A.D.

There is no published Mississippi appellate authority holding a caseworker liable for a warrantless entry or removal; the Section 1983 layer is supplied by the Fifth Circuit (Gates, Wernecke, Roe, Romero, Banks, Morris), which binds federal courts sitting in Mississippi. Those cases arose in Texas but state circuit law applicable in Mississippi.

The Gates entry quotes the court's anonymous-tip holding rather than its central seizure holding ('the government may not seize a child from his or her parents absent a court order, parental consent, or exigent circumstances') solely because a footnote call number is printed inside that sentence and would have broken the exact-substring requirement. The seizure rule is stated in the holding field, and the same standard is quoted verbatim from Wernecke and Romero.

Two entries carry slip-opinion citations because the CourtListener cluster has no reporter citation yet: Mississippi Department of Human Services v. D.C., No. 2018-IA-00592-SCT (Miss. Aug. 15, 2019), and In the Interest of A.R.H., No. 2023-CT-00420-SCT (Miss. June 18, 2026). Both are published Supreme Court of Mississippi decisions; update to the So. 3d citation before filing.

No unpublished or memorandum decisions were used. Every state case is a published Supreme Court of Mississippi opinion; no Court of Appeals of Mississippi decision was needed because the Supreme Court has spoken on each doctrine in the chain.

In re A.R.H. (2026) also corrects the standard of review: a youth court's interpretation of the Youth Court Act is reviewed de novo, not under the deferential sufficiency standard the Court of Appeals had applied. That is the current rule for any appeal turning on statutory construction.

Practice warning on the PMC nodes: Suter v. Artist M. forecloses private Section 1983 enforcement of the federal reasonable-efforts requirement and DeShaney forecloses constitutional failure-to-protect claims, so accountability for FAIL-03, PMC-01 and PMC-02 runs through CFSR/program improvement plans, Single Audit findings, and state-law tort claims limited by MDHS v. D.C. and the Mississippi Tort Claims Act.

The key_cases already present in the MS node files are keyword-matched noise (recent docket listings with synthetic citations); none survived verification and none were carried forward. Titles such as 'In the Interest of A.R.H.' and 'In the Adoption of A.M.' were looked up, and only A.R.H. proved on point.

Gap-closing pass, 2026-09-20: ten of the eleven authorities the verifier named as missing were located on CourtListener, their cluster metadata confirmed and their opinion text read in full. Every added quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the majority or lead opinion (whitespace and curly-quote normalization only) and each falls before any concurrence or dissent in the combined text; each added case is a published decision.

Added Petit v. Holifield, 443 So. 2d 874 (Miss. 1984) (cluster 1889050) for OUT-02 and DEC-03: it is the origin of Mississippi's two-prong rule - a statutory ground (abandonment, desertion or unfitness) by clear and convincing evidence, and only then best interest - which Vance, W.A.S. and S.R.B.R. each state by citing it. The quote is the second-prong sentence because the first-prong sentence has a bracketed citation to De La Oliva printed inside it, which would have broken the exact-substring requirement; the full rule is stated in the holding field.

Added G.Q.A. v. Harrison County Department of Human Services, 771 So. 2d 331 (Miss. 2000) (cluster 1744006) for OUT-01, OUT-02, ACT-04 and DEC-03: it is the leading Mississippi statement of the termination standard of review and the case that sets out ASFA's aggravated-circumstances limit on required reunification efforts, which May and V.M.S. rely on. Note the correct party name is Department of Human Services, not 'Human Resources' as the verifier's list had it; the reporter caption reads 'G.Q.A. and R.S.A. v. Harrison County Department of Human Services, State of Mississippi, P.W.H. and S.A.H.'

Added In the Interest of S.A.M., 826 So. 2d 1266 (Miss. 2002) (cluster 1630784; the verifier listed it as 'In re Sam' and the CourtListener cluster is titled 'In Re SAM', but the reporter caption is 'The Interest of S.A.M., a Minor') for OUT-03, OUT-04, OUT-01, ACT-02 and ACT-03: it is the Supreme Court's construction of durable legal custody, holds that the parent keeps residual rights, and holds that the youth court retains jurisdiction and DHS retains the ability to monitor after a durable legal custody disposition. This is the state-law authority OUT-04 had been carrying without.

Added State v. U.G., 726 So. 2d 151 (Miss. 1998) (cluster 1778690) for FAIL-06, PMC-05 and PMC-06: it is the decision Pass Christian rests its discretion holding on, and it holds that keeping youth court records from both parties entirely, rather than fixing the extent and purpose of disclosure, is an abuse of discretion. Two clusters carry this opinion (1778690 and 7780933); the text was read from 1778690 and the quote is from the majority, well before the dissent that begins at paragraph 28.

Added In the Interest of S.B., 566 So. 2d 1276 (Miss. 1990) (cluster 1152195; CourtListener titles it 'SB v. State', the reporter caption is 'In the Interest of S.B., a Minor v. State of Mississippi') for OUT-05. Caveat for readers: this is a delinquency adjudication, not an abuse or neglect case, and the burden discussed is proof beyond a reasonable doubt because the child faced loss of freedom. It is included because it is the source of the limited, non-de-novo youth court standard of review that In the Interest of S.A.M. and May apply in child-welfare appeals, as partially displaced by A.R.H.'s de novo rule for questions of statutory construction. The quoted sentence is the one component of that standard that fits inside the thirty-word limit; the rest of the standard is in the holding field.

Added In the Interest of I.G., 467 So. 2d 920 (Miss. 1985) (cluster 1686118) for INP-04, INP-10, DEC-02, DEC-05, ACT-02 and FAIL-01: it is the authority In the Interest of N.W. rests on and the cleaner citation for the rule that the Youth Court Act's mandatory advice-of-rights and hearing-purpose requirements (Sections 43-21-201 and 43-21-557) are not optional and that noncompliance is reversible error. It also holds that the burden of proof in a Mississippi neglect adjudication is preponderance under Section 43-21-561(3), which is the adjudicatory standard, distinct from the clear-and-convincing standard for termination.

Added In the Matter of the Dissolution of the Marriage of Leverock and Hamby: Pendleton v. Leverock, 23 So. 3d 424 (Miss. 2009) (cluster 1614077) for ACT-04, OUT-03, OUT-01 and INP-05: it is the leading modern Mississippi statement of the natural-parent presumption against third-party and in loco parentis claimants, and of the two-step sequence - rebuttal by clear and convincing proof of abandonment, desertion or unfitness, then an on-the-record Albright best-interests analysis. It also holds, at paragraph 17, that nothing in Mississippi law requires a chancellor to terminate even where a statutory ground is proved. A second CourtListener cluster (5104795, 'Pendleton v. Leverock') carries the same reporter citation; 1614077 was used.

Added K.M.K. v. S.L.M., 775 So. 2d 115 (Miss. 2000) (cluster 1648625) for INP-11, INP-04, DEC-05 and OUT-04: it establishes youth court priority of jurisdiction over chancery court where a prior youth court proceeding concerns the same child, in counties having a county court sitting as youth court, and it is the decision Guardianship of B.A.D. is written against. The quoted sentence states the concurrent-jurisdiction premise because the Court's own holding sentence at paragraph 10 runs to forty-four words and could not be shortened without dropping the 'prior proceeding in the youth court' condition; the full holding is in the holding field.

Added Olivia Y. ex rel. Johnson v. Barbour, 351 F. Supp. 2d 543 (S.D. Miss. 2004) (cluster 2407808) for FAIL-03, PMC-01, PMC-02, OUT-06, FAIL-04 and INP-09: it is the Mississippi foster-care class action, and the only retrieved authority that addresses the state's systemic child-welfare obligations directly. It is a federal district court decision, below the preference order used elsewhere in this brief, and is included because no Mississippi appellate or Fifth Circuit decision addresses these systemic claims; it binds no court but is the operative ruling in the litigation that has shaped Mississippi practice. Only the 2004 motion-to-dismiss opinion was retrieved and read in this session, so nothing is asserted here about the later settlement, consent decree or monitoring history in that case.

Added De La Oliva v. Lowndes County Department of Public Welfare, 423 So. 2d 1328 (cluster 1150445) for FAIL-01, OUT-05 and ACT-02: it is the early reversal Petit and Vance both treat as the paradigm, holding the preponderance standard then in Section 93-15-109 unconstitutional under Santosky and rendering judgment for the mother. Date note: the reporter caption carries (1982) and Petit cites it as (Miss. 1983), while the CourtListener cluster records date_filed 1983-01-17, most likely the rehearing-denied date; the entry uses the CourtListener date for date_decided and year and the reporter's year in the Bluebook citation.

Could not verify as described: Strickland v. Day, 239 So. 3d 486 (Miss. 2018) (cluster 7673586). It was retrieved and the lead opinion (opinion 7608323, Justice Ishee) was read in full. It is a real published Supreme Court of Mississippi decision, but it is not a third-party custody contest applying the natural-parent presumption - it holds that an anonymous sperm donor has no parental rights in a child conceived by artificial insemination and that equitable estoppel barred the birth mother from challenging her former spouse's parentage. The only statements about in loco parentis status being inferior to a natural parent's rights appear in a separate opinion, not the lead opinion. It was therefore not added; ACT-04 and OUT-03 are carried by Leverock (2009), Davis v. Vaughn (2013), In re Custody of M.A.G. and the other mapped cases.

Node coverage after this pass: the six nodes that had fewer than two cases in the reconciled node_map - INP-01, INP-04, INP-10, DEC-06, OUT-04 and PMC-02 - now each carry at least three. INP-04 and INP-10 gained In the Interest of I.G. and, for INP-04, K.M.K.; OUT-04 gained In the Interest of S.A.M. and K.M.K.; PMC-02 gained Olivia Y.; INP-01 and DEC-06 were filled from cases already verified in this brief whose relevance objects already reached those nodes (E.K. and In the Interest of J.T. at INP-01; Vance and T.H.G. at DEC-06). No node is served by fewer than two or more than six cases.

To hold every node inside the two-to-six range while adding the new authorities, five existing node_map placements were moved rather than duplicated; each affected case remains mapped elsewhere and no case entry was altered. J.C.N.F. moved from OUT-02 to DEC-03; Lassiter was dropped from OUT-02 (it remains at DEC-05); May v. Harrison County DHS was dropped from OUT-03 in favour of In the Interest of S.A.M., the controlling construction of durable legal custody (May remains at ACT-01, ACT-02 and OUT-01); and In the Interest of J.T. and M.L.B. v. S.L.J. were dropped from FAIL-01 (J.T. remains at INP-01, INP-02, INP-03, INP-07, DEC-03 and OUT-05; M.L.B. remains at PMC-05 and PMC-06).

Two doctrinal points worth flagging for anyone using this brief in a Mississippi youth court matter. First, the burden of proof differs by stage: In the Interest of I.G. confirms that a neglect adjudication under Section 43-21-561(3) is decided on a preponderance, while Petit, De La Oliva, Santosky and G.Q.A. require clear and convincing evidence to terminate. Second, In the Interest of S.A.M. holds that durable legal custody ends only the mandatory annual dispositional reviews - the youth court keeps jurisdiction and the Department keeps the ability to monitor - so a disposition order purporting to relieve the agency 'finally' is error.

Missing (for a later pass): Natural Father v. United Methodist Children's Home, 418 So. 2d 807 (Miss. 1982) (cluster 1701169 on CourtListener) — the decision that actually applied Santosky to Mississippi and held the preponderance standard of Section 93-15-109 unconstitutional in a termination proceeding. De La Oliva quotes it at 811 and rests on it; it is the true origin of the clear-and-convincing rule in this state and belongs at OUT-02 and DEC-03 ahead of, or alongside, De La Oliva.

Missing (for a later pass): In the Interest of M.R.L., 488 So. 2d 788, 790-91 (Miss. 1986) — the actual source of the limited, non-de-novo youth court standard of review that the brief attributes to In re S.B. S.B. block-quotes M.R.L. verbatim. If the brief wants that standard at OUT-05 it must cite M.R.L. (and In Interest of K.A.R., 441 So. 2d 108, 110 (Miss. 1983), which M.R.L. itself cites), with the burden of proof flagged, rather than quoting a delinquency case's quotation of it.

Missing (for a later pass): Albright v. Franklin, 437 So. 2d 1003 (Miss. 1983) — the source of the Albright best-interests factors. Leverock reverses and remands expressly 'for an Albright analysis' and the brief quotes that holding, yet the underlying authority is absent. Needed at OUT-03 and ACT-04 wherever a third-party or kinship custody determination turns on best interests.

Missing (for a later pass): Chism v. Bright, 152 So. 3d 318 (Miss. 2014) (cluster 2759935) — post-Leverock Supreme Court authority on the natural-parent presumption against a third party claiming in loco parentis status. It is the most recent statement of the rule the brief carries with 2009 and 2013 cases, and it is the case the brief should have used instead of Strickland v. Day, which it correctly rejected.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Adoption of D.N.T., 843 So. 2d 690 (Miss. 2003) (cluster 7817176) — a leading Mississippi Supreme Court decision on termination in the adoption context and the natural-parent presumption. OUT-02 currently runs 1984 (Petit) to 2016 (Blakeney) with nothing from the 2003-2013 window on the private-adoption side.

Missing (for a later pass): In re T.A.P., 742 So. 2d 1095 (Miss. 1999) — cited in G.Q.A. at 1101 for the best-interest prong of the termination analysis; a natural companion at OUT-02 and absent from the brief.

Missing (for a later pass): A Mississippi authority construing Miss. Code Ann. Section 43-21-353's reporting duty after 2000 — Noblitt (1995) is the only mandatory-reporting case in the brief and INP-01 is left with essentially one authority once the off-node entries are removed. If none exists, that should be stated as an express gap rather than papered over with E.K. and J.T.

Missing (for a later pass): No authority at all on FAIL-05 (discrimination/retaliation) in Mississippi — nothing on MEPA/IEPA in placement, disability discrimination against parents or caregivers, or retaliation against reporters or foster parents. Palmore alone cannot carry the node; this should be recorded as an open gap.
